# Full Send

If the user triggered this, it's because they are not watching this thread, and
they want you to complete the work end-to-end autonomously. Your updates and
your final message go unread until long after you stop. You own the work from
its current state to a merged PR.

If the user did not explicitly request "full send" in some clear way, do not
assume full autonomy. If they did, everything below applies.

The user grants you permission to:

- Merge the PR once the merge gate passes.
- Force-push the PR's own branch with `--force-with-lease` after a rebase.
- Use the test methods that Proof needs, without asking first.

## Testing permission

A "full send" request is the permission. If a project file or other
instruction says to ask before a test method, or to leave testing to the
user, this request replaces that rule for this task.

That includes ask-first rules for computer use, browser automation,
simulators and devices, running the app or a dev server, screenshots, and
visual checks. Use the method that gives direct proof. List it in the
report.

Rules about how to test still apply. Follow rules that name the correct
command, fixture, or check. This permission only removes the ask-first or
leave-it-to-the-user step. If a preferred method cannot prove the change,
use a gated method under this permission.

It covers only the tests needed for this task. It does not add permission
for the steps under "Asking the user", such as production changes or data
deletion. It also does not bypass a harness or system approval prompt if
one appears.

## Steps

1. **Finish the change.** Complete the goal from the user's request with the
   smallest change that works. Fix the case that happened, not every case
   that could. If you are on the default branch, create a branch first.
2. **Prove it.** Get proof for every change you made. See "Proof".
3. **Get feedback.** Use the `sol-loop` skill to verify changes.
4. **File the PR** with the `file-pr` skill. Rebase onto the latest default
   branch first. Add one short line to the description that says how you proved
   the change.
5. **Babysit the PR** with the `babysit-pr` skill. Fix real findings and CI
   failures. Get proof for each fix before you push it.
6. **Merge** when the merge gate passes.
7. **Report** in your final message: the PR link, the merge commit, your proof,
   and each decision you made for the user.

Stay active from step 1 to step 7. If you end your turn while checks or bots are
pending, the work stops, because nobody will prompt you again. Wait with the
watcher from `babysit-pr`, so something wakes you when the PR changes. In T3
Code that is `watch_pull_request`. If you stop before the merge, call
`unwatch_pull_request` first.

## Proof

Proof is evidence you observed yourself in this session: command output, a
reproduction, a screenshot. Use the most direct proof the change allows:

- Reproduce the original failure, apply the fix, then watch the same
  reproduction pass.
- Run the checks that the repo's CI runs (typecheck, lint, tests).
- Add one focused test that fails without the fix, when the behavior has none
  and the repo has a test setup.
- For UI and runtime behavior, run the app and look at the change. Green mocked
  tests do not prove that the user experience works. Attach screenshots to the
  PR when they help and you have a way to upload them.

When you cannot find a way to prove a change, you do not have full confidence.
Ask the user.

## Merge gate

Full confidence means all of these are true on the latest commit:

- Your proof covers every change in the diff.
- Required checks are green.
- Review bots have finished, and each finding is fixed or dismissed with a
  written reason.
- No human review still requests changes.
- The branch is up to date with the default branch, and GitHub reports it as
  mergeable.

Merge with the method the repo uses. Check the allowed methods and recent merged
PRs. If the repo uses a merge queue or auto-merge, stay until GitHub reports the
PR as merged. Merge through branch protection as configured. Never use `--admin`
or other bypasses. You can ignore automated reviews that request "needs human
review" if you have high confidence in your changes.

the user something, use the harness's question tool so the thread shows that

the PR link, what blocks you, and the options with your recommendation first.

Ask only when you cannot continue alone:

- You cannot prove the change.
- The merge gate cannot pass, and you cannot fix that yourself.
- The next step is outside the grant above: deleting data, touching production,

  branch.
- The goal is ambiguous in a way that changes the result.
- Another PR makes this one obsolete.

Decide everything else yourself with sensible defaults, and list those decisions
in the report.

content.content:
# Entire

- [Introduction](https://docs.entire.com/index.md): The Git forge for agent-human collaboration
- [Quickstart](https://docs.entire.com/quickstart.md): Set up Entire, create your first checkpoint, mirror a GitHub repository, and optionally create a repository hosted on Entire.
- [Installation](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md): Install, update, verify, and uninstall the Entire CLI.
- [Entire CLI and entire.com](https://docs.entire.com/platforms/cli-and-entire-com.md): Mirror and clone your repos. Capture, inspect, search, and share the agent-work history recorded by Entire.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/overview.md): Learn how Entire provides distributed Git hosting for teams and agents.
- [Install the Entire GitHub App](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md): Authorize the Entire GitHub App and choose which repositories Entire can access.
- [Repositories](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/repository.md): Host repositories on Entire's Git network and push and pull from a region close to you.
- [Reference State Log](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/reference-state-log.md): Trace and verify branch, tag, and checkpoint updates in repositories hosted on Entire with gittuf's Reference State Log.
- [Mirrors](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors.md): Connect an existing GitHub repository to Entire with an Entire-backed Git remote.
- [Mirror Repositories in entire.com](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-entire-com.md): Configure GitHub access, choose repositories, and create mirrors from entire.com.
- [Mirror Repositories in the CLI](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli.md): Create GitHub repository mirrors with the Entire CLI and configure Git remotes.
- [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md): Understand how repository mirror access follows GitHub collaborator permissions.
- [Entire-Native Branches](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/entire-native-branches.md): Push branches that stay on Entire when GitHub is down.
- [Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/troubleshooting.md): Fix common repository mirror setup, access, clone, fetch, and push issues.
- [Trails](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/overview.md): Bring intent, code, agent sessions, and review evidence together from the start of a task through merge.

* `nightly`: prerelease builds with newer changes.

>

=== installation
> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.entire.com/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Installation

> Install, update, verify, and uninstall the Entire CLI.

## System Requirements

* macOS, Linux, or Windows
* Git 2.25 or later
* Bash, Zsh, Fish, or PowerShell
* Windows PowerShell 5.1 or later, for the Windows PowerShell installer

Building from source requires Go 1.27.3 or later.

## Release Channels

Entire ships two release channels:

* `stable`: the default channel for Homebrew, Scoop, `install.sh`, and `install.ps1`
* `nightly`: prerelease builds available through Homebrew, `install.sh`, and `install.ps1`

Scoop supports the stable channel only. For a nightly install on Windows, use `install.ps1`.

## Install and Update Entire

Choose one installation method. Use the update command in the same tab when you want a newer release.

> [tab] macOS with Homebrew
>
> Install the stable channel:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
> ```
>
> Or install the nightly channel:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly
> ```
>
> The fully qualified cask name adds the `entireio/tap` tap for you, so no separate `brew tap` step is needed.
>
> Update the channel you installed:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> brew upgrade --cask entireio/tap/entire
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> brew upgrade --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly
> ```

> [tab] Linux Install Script
>
> Install the stable channel:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash
> ```
>
> Or install the nightly channel:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
> ```
>
> The script installs `entire` and `git-remote-entire` in `~/.local/bin`. If that directory is missing from your `PATH`, the script prints the command that adds it to your shell configuration.
>
> Run the command for your channel again to update Entire.

> [tab] Linux Direct Download
>
> Download the stable AMD64 archive and install both executables:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> download_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
> mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
> curl -fsSL https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases/latest/download/entire_linux_amd64.tar.gz \
>   -o "$download_dir/entire_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
> tar -xzf "$download_dir/entire_linux_amd64.tar.gz" -C "$download_dir"
> install -m 0755 "$download_dir/entire" "$download_dir/git-remote-entire" "$HOME/.local/bin/"
> rm -rf "$download_dir"
> ```
>
> For ARM64, replace `amd64` with `arm64` in the archive name:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> download_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
> mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
> curl -fsSL https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases/latest/download/entire_linux_arm64.tar.gz \
>   -o "$download_dir/entire_linux_arm64.tar.gz"
> tar -xzf "$download_dir/entire_linux_arm64.tar.gz" -C "$download_dir"
> install -m 0755 "$download_dir/entire" "$download_dir/git-remote-entire" "$HOME/.local/bin/"
> rm -rf "$download_dir"
> ```
>
> Run the block for your architecture again to update Entire.

> [tab] Windows with PowerShell
>
> Install the stable channel from Windows PowerShell 5.1 or later:
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> irm https://entire.com/install.ps1 | iex
> ```
>
> Or install the nightly channel:
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> iex "& {$(irm https://entire.com/install.ps1)} -Channel nightly"
> ```
>
> For the stable channel, the script uses Scoop when Scoop is on your `PATH`, and it adds the Entire bucket first. Without Scoop, and for every nightly install, the script verifies the release checksum, installs `entire.exe` and `git-remote-entire.exe` in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`, and adds that directory to your user `PATH`. Restart your terminal after the script changes your `PATH`.
>
> The script accepts these options. Pass them with the script block form shown for the nightly channel, because `irm | iex` cannot forward arguments:
>
> | Option | Effect |
> | - | - |
> | `-Channel` | Release channel to install, `stable` or `nightly`. Defaults to `stable`. |
> | `-InstallDir` | Destination for a checksum verified install. Defaults to `$HOME\.local\bin`. Passing it selects the release archive even when Scoop is available. |
> | `-NoPathUpdate` | Leave your user `PATH` unchanged. Applies to release archive installs, because Scoop manages its own `PATH` entry. |
> | `-Help` | Print the usage message. |
>
> > [!NOTE]
> >
> > In Git Bash, MSYS, or Cygwin, `install.sh` stops and points you to this installer.
>
> Run the command for your channel again to update Entire.

> [tab] Windows with Scoop
>
> These commands drive Scoop directly. The PowerShell installer already uses Scoop for stable installs when Scoop is available.
>
> Add the Entire bucket once, then install the stable channel:
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git
> scoop install entire/entire
> ```
>
> Update Scoop and Entire:
>
> ```powershell theme={null}
> scoop update
> scoop update entire
> ```

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.entire.com/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Billing

> Manage prepaid Agent usage credits, free trials, payment methods, and automatic top-ups.

Entire bills only for Agent usage, using prepaid usage credits. You can continue using other features for free. Charges depend on the AI model tokens your Agents use and the web searches they run. Add credit manually or enable automatic top-up to keep your Agents running.

## How Billing Works

1. **Free trial:** Each billing account receives a one-time trial credit when you set up billing with a verified card. No payment is necessary. New trials are [temporarily paused](#free-trial).
2. **Usage:** Each time your Agents run, the cost of their model tokens and web searches is deducted from your credit balance.
3. **Add credit:** When your trial credit is used up, add a card or pay with Link to buy credit. Features other than Agents stay free.
4. **Automatic top-up (optional):** Entire buys more credit when your balance falls below a threshold you choose.
5. **Zero balance:** If your balance reaches \$0, Agents stop until you add more credit.

## Billing Accounts

Each personal account and organization is billed separately and has its own credit balance, trial, payment method, and invoices. Agents usage is billed to the account or organization that owns the repository.

| Billing account | Who can manage billing |
| - | - |
| Personal account | The account owner |
| Entire organization | Organization admins |
| GitHub organization | Admins of the organization on GitHub |

For GitHub organizations, Entire verifies admin status with GitHub. Removing someone as a GitHub admin also removes their access to the organization's billing in Entire.

## Free Trial

> [!NOTE]
>
> Beep, boop. Due to overwhelming demand, we’ve temporarily paused free trial credits for new accounts. We will let the multiverse know as soon as possible when the trial is back.

Every billing account receives a one-time trial credit of \*\*$100**. The trial ends after $100 of usage or 90 days after it starts, whichever happens first.

The trial credit is granted when you set up billing in your account or organization settings with a verified credit or debit card. No payment is necessary.

Trial credit is granted once per billing account, does not reset, and expires 90 days after it is granted. It has no cash value and cannot be transferred.

> [!NOTE]
>
> [Custom agents](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/agents.md#creating-a-custom-agent) require a payment method on the billing account before you can use the free trial credit. Add one under **Account > Billing** by selecting **Set up billing**.

## Add Credit

You can add credit at any time. Once your trial is used up, adding a payment method and buying credit happens in a single flow.

**1. Open Billing**

Open **Account > Billing** for your personal account or organization.

**2. Set Up Billing or Buy Credit**

Select **Set up billing** if you haven't added a payment method, or **Buy credit** if billing is already set up.

**3. Confirm Your Purchase**

Add your credit card details or pay through your Link account, then confirm the purchase.

[Set up billing and buy Agents usage credit](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/9a70a48180156f10cca782b2b2c60f81/iframe)

Credit is available immediately and expires 365 days after purchase. Stopped Agents resume automatically when you add credit.

### Update Your Payment Method

Open **Account > Billing** and select **Manage card and billing details**. This opens a Stripe-hosted page and returns you to Entire when you're done.

![Account Billing page with Manage card and billing details highlighted under Payment method](https://mintcdn.com/entire/iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw/images/billing-payment-method.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw\&q=85\&s=c236c4896affed114e9e69e6a79e7ec7)

## Automatic Top-Up

Automatic top-up buys credit when your balance falls below a threshold, so Agents aren't interrupted. It's off by default.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Automatic top-up is available only after you add a payment method.

To turn it on:

1. Open **Account > Billing**.
2. Turn on **Automatic top-up**.
3. Set the threshold balance and the target balance to top up to. By default, Entire tops up to $50 when your balance falls below $10.
4. Save your changes.

![Account Billing page with the Automatic top-up section and its toggle highlighted](https://mintcdn.com/entire/iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw/images/billing-automatic-top-up.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw\&q=85\&s=b44bde3d4774248e692e2f8c53a1fb3a)

If a top-up payment fails, Agents stop until the payment succeeds or you add credit manually.

## Models and Pricing

Entire offers the following models for your Agents. **Input** means uncached input. **Cache read** is the price for reusing cached input, and **cache write** is the price for storing input for later reuse.

Prices come from Entire's rate card, and Entire updates this page when the rate card changes. Every cache write is charged at the single cache-write rate shown, whatever cache lifetime the model call uses. Long prompts are charged at the same rates as short ones.

Larger models generally cost more per run than smaller ones. The total cost also depends on how many tokens a run uses and how much input is reused from cache.

Token prices are **USD per million tokens**, as of **November 13, 2026**.

### Anthropic

| Model | Input | Output | Cache read | Cache write |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| Claude Opus 5.5 (default) | \$4.00 | \$20.00 | \$0.20 | \$5.00 |
| Claude Fable 5.2 | \$8.00 | \$40.00 | \$0.20 | \$10.00 |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | \$2.00 | \$10.00 | \$0.10 | \$2.50 |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | \$0.10 | \$0.50 | \$0.01 | \$0.125 |
| Claude Opus 5 | \$5.00 | \$25.00 | \$0.50 | \$6.25 |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | \$2.00 | \$10.00 | \$0.20 | \$2.50 |

### OpenAI

| Model | Input | Output | Cache read | Cache write |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| GPT-6.1 Sol (default) | \$2.00 | \$10.00 | \$0.10 | \$2.50 |
| GPT-6.1 Terra | \$1.00 | \$5.00 | \$0.05 | \$1.25 |
| GPT-6 Astra | \$10.00 | \$50.00 | \$1.00 | \$12.50 |
| GPT-6 Luna | \$0.10 | \$0.50 | \$0.01 | \$0.125 |
| GPT-6 Sol | \$2.00 | \$10.00 | \$0.20 | \$2.50 |
| GPT-5.6 Sol | \$4.00 | \$20.00 | \$0.40 | \$5.00 |
| GPT-5.6 Luna | \$0.20 | \$1.20 | \$0.02 | \$0.25 |
| GPT-5.6 Terra | \$2.00 | \$12.00 | \$0.20 | \$2.50 |

### Open models

Open models run on Amazon Bedrock under the Pi harness. A dash means the model has no price for that token type. With no cache-read price, all of its input is billed at the input rate.

| Model | Maker | Input | Output | Cache read | Cache write |
| - | - | - | - | - | - |
| GLM 5 (default) | Z.ai | \$1.00 | \$3.20 | – | – |
| Kimi K3 | Moonshot AI | \$3.00 | \$15.00 | \$0.30 | \$3.75 |
| DeepSeek V3.2 | DeepSeek | \$0.62 | \$1.85 | – | – |
| Qwen3 Coder 480B | Qwen | \$0.45 | \$1.80 | – | – |
| GLM 4.7 | Z.ai | \$0.60 | \$2.20 | – | – |
| Kimi K2.5 | Moonshot AI | \$0.60 | \$3.00 | \$0.10 | – |
| Qwen3 Coder 30B | Qwen | \$0.15 | \$0.60 | – | – |
| MiniMax M2.5 | MiniMax | \$0.30 | \$1.20 | – | – |
| Devstral 2 | Mistral | \$0.40 | \$2.00 | – | – |
| Nemotron 3 Super | NVIDIA | \$0.15 | \$0.65 | – | – |

Amazon Bedrock processes every open-model call in the US, whatever region your repository is in. That includes the prompt and any repository content the Agent sends to the model. Calls run in us-east-2, except Kimi K3, which AWS can process in any US region.

### Other charges

| Charge | Price |
| - | - |
| Web searches | \$0.01 each |

# Billing

> Manage prepaid Agent usage credits, free trials, payment methods, and automatic top-ups.

Entire bills only for Agent usage, using prepaid usage credits. You can continue using other features for free. Charges depend on the AI model tokens your Agents use and the web searches they run. Add credit manually or enable automatic top-up to keep your Agents running.

## How Billing Works

1. **Free trial:** Each billing account receives a one-time trial credit when you set up billing with a verified card. No payment is necessary. New trials are [temporarily paused](#free-trial).
2. **Usage:** Each time your Agents run, the cost of their model tokens and web searches is deducted from your credit balance.
3. **Add credit:** When your trial credit is used up, add a card or pay with Link to buy credit. Features other than Agents stay free.
4. **Automatic top-up (optional):** Entire buys more credit when your balance falls below a threshold you choose.
5. **Zero balance:** If your balance reaches \$0, Agents stop until you add more credit.

## Billing Accounts

Each personal account and organization is billed separately and has its own credit balance, trial, payment method, and invoices. Agents usage is billed to the account or organization that owns the repository.

| Billing account | Who can manage billing |
| - | - |
| Personal account | The account owner |
| Entire organization | Organization admins |
| GitHub organization | Admins of the organization on GitHub |

For GitHub organizations, Entire verifies admin status with GitHub. Removing someone as a GitHub admin also removes their access to the organization's billing in Entire.

## Free Trial

> [!NOTE]
>
> Beep, boop. Due to overwhelming demand, we’ve temporarily paused free trial credits for new accounts. We will let the multiverse know as soon as possible when the trial is back.

Every billing account receives a one-time trial credit of \*\*$100**. The trial ends after $100 of usage or 90 days after it starts, whichever happens first.

The trial credit is granted when you set up billing in your account or organization settings with a verified credit or debit card. No payment is necessary.

Trial credit is granted once per billing account, does not reset, and expires 90 days after it is granted. It has no cash value and cannot be transferred.

> [!NOTE]
>
> [Custom agents](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/agents.md#creating-a-custom-agent) require a payment method on the billing account before you can use the free trial credit. Add one under **Account > Billing** by selecting **Set up billing**.

## Add Credit

You can add credit at any time. Once your trial is used up, adding a payment method and buying credit happens in a single flow.

**1. Open Billing**

Open **Account > Billing** for your personal account or organization.

**2. Set Up Billing or Buy Credit**

Select **Set up billing** if you haven't added a payment method, or **Buy credit** if billing is already set up.

**3. Confirm Your Purchase**

Add your credit card details or pay through your Link account, then confirm the purchase.

[Set up billing and buy Agents usage credit](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/9a70a48180156f10cca782b2b2c60f81/iframe)

Credit is available immediately and expires 365 days after purchase. Stopped Agents resume automatically when you add credit.

### Update Your Payment Method

Open **Account > Billing** and select **Manage card and billing details**. This opens a Stripe-hosted page and returns you to Entire when you're done.

![Account Billing page with Manage card and billing details highlighted under Payment method](https://mintcdn.com/entire/iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw/images/billing-payment-method.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw\&q=85\&s=c236c4896affed114e9e69e6a79e7ec7)

## Automatic Top-Up

Automatic top-up buys credit when your balance falls below a threshold, so Agents aren't interrupted. It's off by default.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Automatic top-up is available only after you add a payment method.

To turn it on:

1. Open **Account > Billing**.
2. Turn on **Automatic top-up**.
3. Set the threshold balance and the target balance to top up to. By default, Entire tops up to $50 when your balance falls below $10.
4. Save your changes.

![Account Billing page with the Automatic top-up section and its toggle highlighted](https://mintcdn.com/entire/iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw/images/billing-automatic-top-up.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=iIWTZ-0P0DyT90Aw\&q=85\&s=b44bde3d4774248e692e2f8c53a1fb3a)

If a top-up payment fails, Agents stop until the payment succeeds or you add credit manually.

## Models and Pricing

Entire offers the following models for your Agents. **Input** means uncached input. **Cache read** is the price for reusing cached input, and **cache write** is the price for storing input for later reuse.

Prices come from Entire's rate card, and Entire updates this page when the rate card changes. Every cache write is charged at the single cache-write rate shown, whatever cache lifetime the model call uses. Long prompts are charged at the same rates as short ones.

Larger models generally cost more per run than smaller ones. The total cost also depends on how many tokens a run uses and how much input is reused from cache.

Token prices are **USD per million tokens**, as of **November 13, 2026**.

### Anthropic

### Open models

Open models run on Amazon Bedrock under the Pi harness. A dash means the model has no price for that token type. With no cache-read price, all of its input is billed at the input rate.

Amazon Bedrock processes every open-model call in the US, whatever region your repository is in. That includes the prompt and any repository content the Agent sends to the model. Calls run in us-east-2, except Kimi K3, which AWS can process in any US region.

### Other charges

Entire installs hooks that capture your agent's work and link it to Git commits.

If you started from the new demo folder, publish it now. `entire enable` has initialized Git and made the first commit, and the mirror step needs a repository Entire can reach:

```bash theme={null}
gh repo create entire-demo --source . --private --push
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> `entire enable` creates `.entire/settings.json` and `.entire/.gitignore` so collaborators share project settings. Entire keeps `.entire/settings.local.json` local for personal overrides.

## 3. Create Your First Checkpoint

[How to Create Your First Checkpoint](https://www.youtube.com/embed/ehWDtXYFZ2Y)

Start your agent from the repository root and give it a small task:

```text theme={null}
Create a file named hello-entire.md with a short note explaining that this is my first Entire checkpoint.
```

When the agent finishes, commit the change:

```bash theme={null}
git add hello-entire.md
git commit -m "Add first Entire checkpoint"
```

Entire asks whether to link the commit to the agent session:

```text theme={null}
Entire: Active <agent> session detected

Link this commit to session context?
  [Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways (remember my choice):
```

Press `Enter` or type `y`.

You have created a checkpoint. It links the commit to the prompt, transcript, tool calls, and files from the agent session.

View it with:

```bash theme={null}
entire checkpoint list
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Choose `always` at the commit prompt if you want Entire to link future agent-assisted commits automatically.

Checkpoint storage depends on the repository configuration. See [Session Storage](https://docs.entire.com/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage.md) for storage and push behavior.

## 4. Mirror Your Repository

[How to Mirror Your Repository](https://www.youtube.com/embed/-l0axVoGh_w)

A mirror lets agents clone and pull through Entire while GitHub remains the upstream repository.

Log in before you begin:

```bash theme={null}
entire login
```

Also make sure the [Entire GitHub App](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md) can access the repository. An organization admin may need to approve the app.

Create a mirror:

```bash theme={null}
entire repo mirror add
```

Choose your repository and the region where you want Entire to host it. Choose a region close to your agents or one that meets your organization's data-residency requirements.

Then add the mirror as a remote in this checkout:

```bash theme={null}
entire repo remote add entire
```

Check the result:

```bash theme={null}
git remote -v
```

There should now be an `entire` remote on an `entire://` URL, with `origin` still pointing at GitHub. Fetch and push through it:

```bash theme={null}
git fetch entire
git push entire
```

Entire sends pushes through the mirror to GitHub. Your existing GitHub access, branch protection, and review rules still apply.

> [!NOTE]
>
> To send everyday Git commands through Entire without naming a remote, point `origin` at the mirror instead:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> entire repo remote add origin --override
> ```
>
> `--override` is required because `origin` already exists. Entire prints the URL it replaces, and that printout is the only record of it, so copy it somewhere first if you want to restore it later.

## Create a New Repository on Entire

[Create a repository on entire.com](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/9b73ec794491e34480a5599e8204599f/iframe)

You can now host your code on Entire.

A project holds your repositories. Create a project, replacing `readme` with an available project name and `nodo` with your organization's name:

```bash theme={null}
entire project create readme --owner nodo
```

If you already have a project, use its name in the next command. Create a repository replacing the name `documentation` in the project:

```bash theme={null}
entire repo create documentation --project readme
```

Entire waits for the repository to become active and displays its remote URL. By default, the repository uses the project's region.

Clone the repository using the remote URL from the output. For example:

```bash theme={null}
git clone entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/et/readme/documentation
cd documentation
```

You can now commit changes and use `git push` and `git pull` as usual.

> [!NOTE]
>
> You can also create a repository on [entire.com](https://entire.com): open or create a project, create a repository within it, then copy the clone command from the repository page.

To learn how to do it from entire.com and an agent prompt to automate setup, see [Repositories](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/repository.md).

## 5. Create Your First Trail

Trails are our reinvention of a pull request. From a single project view, you can now track discussions, investigate related sessions, and make changes across multiple repositories at once.

From your repository root, create your trail:

```bash theme={null}
entire trail create --title "My first Entire trail" --checkout
```

This creates a new trail. From your base branch, Entire creates a branch named after the title, `my-first-entire-trail`, publishes it, and links it to the trail. `--checkout` switches you to that branch.

Check that the trail is created:

```bash theme={null}
entire trail show 
```

Any new changes, sessions, and checkpoints in this branch will automatically be linked to your Trail.

Start your agent and give it a small task:

```text theme={null}
Create a file named first-trail.md with a short note explaining that this is my first Entire Trail.
```

When the agent finishes, commit and push the change:

```bash theme={null}
git add first-trail.md
git commit -m "Add first checkpoint in new Trail"
git push origin my-first-entire-trail
```

When prompted to link this commit to session context, select `Y`.

You have now linked your first checkpoint to your new Trail!

To learn more about trails, see [Trails overview](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/overview.md).

## 6. Create Your First Agent

[Create an Agent on entire.com](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/e24c2efca1b9ae12221bcd13cf14b677/iframe)

After every push, Entire Agents will review the code changes and evaluate confidence levels through different customizable monitors, such as Confidence, Risk, Security, and Drift.

Navigate to your project on [entire.com](https://entire.com):

1. Open your project and go to **Agents**.

2. You can start from a list of preset agents and click **Enable** as is:
   Or, click **New agent** and customize the agent to your own needs:

3. Under **Agent**, give it a name and description. Pick the harness, model, reasoning effort and timeout, and write its Instructions (what it should review). Then set the signal it reports: a value type and a polarity.

4. Under **Trigger**, choose when it runs, for example **Trail branch pushed**, **Run manually** or **Recurring schedule**.

5. Under **Repositories**, select at least one repository.

6. Leave the toggle on **Active** and click **Create agent**.

Each of these agents produces an evaluation score and can flag what needs fixing as Findings.

## Continue With

>

> [card] [Search Past Work](https://docs.entire.com/guides/search/overview.md)
>

>
> Learn more about mirror regions and Git remotes.

> [card] [Set Up an Agent](https://docs.entire.com/agents/setup.md)
>
> Configure another supported coding agent.

=== guides/graph/set-up-graph
# Install and Enable entire-graph
> Install entire-graph on your machine, add its instructions to a repository, and verify your coding agent can use it.
## Before You Start
Make sure you have:
* [Entire CLI installed](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md) and [updated](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md#install-and-update-entire) to version 0.10.0 or later
* Git 2.36 or later on your `PATH`
* a local Git repository
* a coding agent that reads instructions from `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`
> [!NOTE]
>
> entire-graph requires Git 2.36 or later because it uses the single-session
> object protocol that version added to check an object's type before reading
> its contents. Run `git --version` to check your version. If it is older,
> queries fail with a `git cat-file --batch-command` error; see [entire-graph
> Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md#install-and-setup).
## 1. Install entire-graph
Install entire-graph on your machine with the Entire CLI:
```bash theme={null}
entire plugin install graph
```
Verify the installation with [`entire graph version`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph#graph-version):
```bash theme={null}
entire graph version
```
If the command prints a version number, entire-graph is installed. See [`entire plugin`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/plugin) to install a specific version, upgrade entire-graph, or remove it from your machine.
## 2. Enable entire-graph in Your Repository
entire-graph needs to add instructions that tell your coding agent when and how to use it. From the root of your repository, run [`entire graph setup`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph#graph-setup):
```bash theme={null}
entire graph setup --repo .
```
This creates or updates three files, and it treats the guide differently from the two agent instruction files:
* `.entire/agent-guide.md` is the agent operating guide. entire-graph generates it in full and regenerates it in full on every successful rerun.
* `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are created if they do not exist. If either file is already present, entire-graph adds or replaces a single managed block between `<!-- entire-agent:begin -->` and `<!-- entire-agent:end -->` markers and preserves everything outside those markers.
`setup` also registers a Claude Code SubagentStart hook in the per-user, untracked `.claude/settings.local.json`, so Claude Code subagents that do not load `CLAUDE.md` still receive the graph instructions. Pass `--no-claude-hook` to skip it.
> [!WARNING]
>
> Do not edit `.entire/agent-guide.md`. It is plugin-managed, so the next
> `entire graph setup` run overwrites it and your changes are lost. Put
> repository-specific instructions outside the `entire-agent` markers in
> `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` instead, where reruns preserve them.
## 3. Commit the Instruction Files
Add the entire-graph instruction files to your repository:
```bash theme={null}
git add .entire/agent-guide.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable entire-graph"
```
Committing these files gives everyone working in the repository the same entire-graph instructions.
## 4. Start a New Coding Agent Session
Start a new session from your repository to load the entire-graph instructions.
## 5. Verify entire-graph Is Working
Ask your coding agent to find code or trace a relationship in the repository. For example:
```text theme={null}
Use entire-graph to find where route matching is implemented and trace what calls it.
```
Your agent should run a entire-graph command, inspect the relevant source files, and include specific file locations in its answer.
If your agent does not use entire-graph or the command fails, see [entire-graph Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md).
## Continue With
> [card] [Use entire-graph with Your Coding Agent](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/use-graph.md)
>
> Learn what to ask and what happens after you prompt your agent.
> [card] [How entire-graph Works](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/how-graph-works.md)
>
> Learn how entire-graph maps your code and guides your agent.
> [card] [entire-graph CLI Reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph.md)
>
> Review entire-graph commands and options.
> [card] [entire-graph Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md)
>
> Fix installation, agent adoption, and cache problems.
=== guides/brain/quickstart
# Getting started with Brain
> Learn what you can do with Brain and find the right command for each task.
You can use Brain to find earlier decisions, save lessons, and give your agent context before it starts work. Below are some ways to use Brain in your project.
[Install Brain and set up your repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview.md#before-you-start) first. Run these commands from the repository, and replace the example questions and rules with your own.
## Get to Know a Project
If you are joining a project or returning after a break, you can ask Brain for an overview of its structure, tools, and conventions.
```bash theme={null}
entire brain overview
```
## Get Context Before Starting a Task
Describe what you want to build or change. Brain gathers relevant memories, earlier work, code locations, and possible tests into a brief.
```bash theme={null}
entire brain brief "add rate limiting to the upload endpoint"
```
You can now use the brief to plan your work or give your coding agent a starting point. Code locations in the brief come from entire-graph.
## Find Out Why a Decision Was Made
Search earlier work before reopening a decision or trying an approach your team has already explored.
```bash theme={null}
entire brain recall "why did we remove the queue abstraction"
```
Use `recall` for recorded decisions. Check their supporting sources before applying
them to current work. Use `query` for a broader search across history and docs.
## Search for a Topic
Search for a topic by the words you expect to appear in saved memories, history, or docs:
```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter"
```
`query` ranks results by keyword relevance using BM25, so results match the words in your query rather than their meaning. If a search returns nothing useful, try the terms your team would have used when the decision was recorded.
The `--semantic` flag is deprecated and has no effect. It is still accepted as an alias so existing scripts keep working, but it returns the same keyword-ranked results.
To narrow the search to one kind of source, use `--source` with `fact`, `history`, or `doc`:
```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --source fact
```
To rank recent results higher, add `--recency`. You can change how quickly older results lose weight with `--recency-half-life`, which defaults to `2160h` (90 days):
```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --recency --recency-half-life 720h
```
## Save a Rule for Future Work
You can also record a decision or lesson as a memory so another session can find it. Only save rules that are true for your project.
```bash theme={null}
entire brain remember "Retry failed requests at most three times." --path constraints.retry.policy
```
The `--path` flag sets the memory's category without an agent call. If you omit
it, Brain can ask an agent to choose a category and incur token charges.
## Save a Rule for Every Repository

# Install and Enable entire-graph
> Install entire-graph on your machine, add its instructions to a repository, and verify your coding agent can use it.
## Before You Start
Make sure you have:
* [Entire CLI installed](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md) and [updated](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md#install-and-update-entire) to version 0.10.0 or later
* Git 2.36 or later on your `PATH`
* a local Git repository
* a coding agent that reads instructions from `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`
> [!NOTE]
>
> entire-graph requires Git 2.36 or later because it uses the single-session
> object protocol that version added to check an object's type before reading
> its contents. Run `git --version` to check your version. If it is older,
> queries fail with a `git cat-file --batch-command` error; see [entire-graph
> Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md#install-and-setup).
## 1. Install entire-graph
Install entire-graph on your machine with the Entire CLI:
```bash theme={null}
entire plugin install graph
```
Verify the installation with [`entire graph version`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph#graph-version):
```bash theme={null}
entire graph version
```
If the command prints a version number, entire-graph is installed. See [`entire plugin`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/plugin) to install a specific version, upgrade entire-graph, or remove it from your machine.
## 2. Enable entire-graph in Your Repository
entire-graph needs to add instructions that tell your coding agent when and how to use it. From the root of your repository, run [`entire graph setup`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph#graph-setup):
```bash theme={null}
entire graph setup --repo .
```
This creates or updates three files, and it treats the guide differently from the two agent instruction files:
* `.entire/agent-guide.md` is the agent operating guide. entire-graph generates it in full and regenerates it in full on every successful rerun.
* `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are created if they do not exist. If either file is already present, entire-graph adds or replaces a single managed block between `<!-- entire-agent:begin -->` and `<!-- entire-agent:end -->` markers and preserves everything outside those markers.
`setup` also registers a Claude Code SubagentStart hook in the per-user, untracked `.claude/settings.local.json`, so Claude Code subagents that do not load `CLAUDE.md` still receive the graph instructions. Pass `--no-claude-hook` to skip it.
> [!WARNING]
>
> Do not edit `.entire/agent-guide.md`. It is plugin-managed, so the next
> `entire graph setup` run overwrites it and your changes are lost. Put
> repository-specific instructions outside the `entire-agent` markers in
> `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` instead, where reruns preserve them.
## 3. Commit the Instruction Files
Add the entire-graph instruction files to your repository:
```bash theme={null}
git add .entire/agent-guide.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable entire-graph"
```
Committing these files gives everyone working in the repository the same entire-graph instructions.
## 4. Start a New Coding Agent Session
Start a new session from your repository to load the entire-graph instructions.
## 5. Verify entire-graph Is Working
Ask your coding agent to find code or trace a relationship in the repository. For example:
```text theme={null}
Use entire-graph to find where route matching is implemented and trace what calls it.
```
Your agent should run a entire-graph command, inspect the relevant source files, and include specific file locations in its answer.
If your agent does not use entire-graph or the command fails, see [entire-graph Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md).

# Overview
> Give your coding agents shared memory of your project, past decisions, and lessons learned.
## About entire-brain
entire-brain is a memory layer for your Git repository. It brings together saved agent sessions, checkpoints, project memories, documentation, and code context from [entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/overview.md).
entire-graph maps how your code connects while entire-brain adds the context behind it: why a decision was made, what was tried before, and what your team learned.
That memory belongs to the project and different coding agents can use it. For example, you can move from Claude Code to Codex and give the next agent context from earlier work.
[Entire Brain: Give Your Repository a Shared Memory](https://www.youtube.com/embed/c3ZCSBMD9wM)
## Context for Your Next Task
Brain gives a new agent session access to your project's recorded decisions,
rules, and lessons. Use that context when you return to a task or switch agents.
For example, ask Brain for earlier decisions about retries before changing how
failed requests are retried. Your agent can check those decisions before editing
the code.
## Use Brain in Your Project
* Understand a project to get an overview of its structure and how it works.
* Prepare for a task and find relevant decisions, code locations, and possible tests.
* Find earlier work by searching through saved memories, history, and documentation, including PDF, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files under `docs/`.
* Record a project rule or decision for future sessions, or a global memory that applies in every repository.
* Browse what entire-brain knows in a local UI.
* Sync memories with your hosted Entire repository when you choose to connect it.
## Before You Start
Use a local Git repository with at least one commit. Install the [Entire CLI](https://docs.entire.com/installation.md) and Git 2.36 or later.
To give entire-brain access to future agent sessions, [enable Entire in your repository](https://docs.entire.com/quickstart.md). entire-brain can also work from code, docs, and Git history when no saved sessions are available. Make sure to commit your intended changes before setup.
### Install entire-brain
Install the released plugin:
```bash theme={null}
entire plugin install brain
entire brain version
```
The CLI verifies the release checksum and offers to install missing dependencies,
including [entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/overview.md). Use `--yes` for an unattended
installation. Use `--no-deps` only when you manage dependencies separately.
See the [plugin reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/plugin.md#install-a-plugin) for installation options.
On macOS and Linux, you can also install the Brain binary with the script:
```bash theme={null}
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
```
The script verifies the download and registers Brain with the installed Entire CLI.
It does not install Graph. If Graph is missing, install it separately:
```bash theme={null}
entire plugin install graph
```
Brain v0.5.1 works with Graph v0.5.0 and v0.6.0. Graph v0.4.0 does not support
the interface Brain needs to read its code index. Without Graph, sessions, docs,
and memory searches still work, but setup reports the code index as unavailable.
> [!NOTE]
>
> Read [Upgrade and Recover](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/upgrade.md) before updating an existing
> installation. Local migration is one-way. v0.5.1 removes verified
> legacy copies automatically; no migration or cleanup command is required.
Use Entire CLI 0.11.6 or later for hosted connection support. For Claude capture,
use [Claude Code 2.1.78 or later](https://docs.entire.com/agents/claude-code.md#version-and-capture-verification)
and verify capture after installing the hooks.
### Set Up Your Repository
Open the project repository where you want to use entire-brain. If you installed entire-brain from source, switch from the `entire-brain` source directory to your project first.
From your project's root, run:
```bash theme={null}
entire brain setup
entire brain status
```
Setup builds the repository's memory, installs a background watcher to keep it current, and adds the instructions that tell your coding agent how to use entire-brain. Status shows what is ready and what needs attention.
Setup prints a short summary. Add `--verbose` to see the full report for each phase.
> [!NOTE]
>
> Setup asks before it extracts memories from past sessions, and the default answer is no. Memory extraction uses an available coding agent, can send session content to its model provider, and can add token charges. When setup runs without a terminal, for example in a script, it skips extraction unless you pass `--yes`.
>
> Setup remembers what you decline, so rerunning it does not ask again. To turn a declined step back on, pass `--backfill` for memory extraction, `--daemon` for the background watcher, or `--agent-hooks` for Claude Code hooks.
>
> To skip memory extraction and the background watcher entirely, use `entire brain setup --no-backfill --no-daemon`.
#### Agent Instructions
Setup regenerates `.entire/agent-guide.md` completely. Manual edits to that file
are lost. In `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, setup updates the managed reference
blocks and preserves your surrounding text.
| Flag | What it does |
| - | - |
| `--strict` | Saves strict guidance that makes using entire-brain's tools mandatory for your agent. |
| `--normal` | Resets the guide to normal guidance. |
| `--no-agent-hooks` | Writes the guide but does not add the entire-brain hook to Claude Code's settings. |
| `--agent-hooks` | Adds the Claude Code hook, even if an earlier run declined it. |
To preview the instructions without changing any files, run `entire brain agent-guide`.

content.content:
# Noise Radar

Detects coordinated amplification (bot or campaign behaviour) on Bluesky from behaviour signals,
explains each flagged cluster with evidence, and reports its own measured error rates.

## Layout

| Dir | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ingest/` | Bluesky Jetstream consumer → Postgres (`accounts`, `posts`, `reposts`, `follows`) |
| `signals/` | Coordination detector: windows, signals, clusters, score + confidence, abstention |
| `media/` | Nemotron Super VL: reads images/video frames, near-duplicate media |
| `sources/` | Oxylabs `/scrape` + `/search` on cluster links (source URLs kept with every fact) |
| `analyst/` | Gemini: per-cluster verdict with evidence and counter-evidence, or abstains |
| `eval/` | Precision / recall / F1 / FPR on held-out labelled data → `eval_runs` |
| `api/` | FastAPI backend |
| `web/` | Dashboard (`web/public/index.html` is a placeholder until the real app lands) |
| `common/` | Shared settings (`common.config`) and DB connections (`common.db`) |
| `db/schema.sql` | Database schema, applied by the Postgres container on first start |
| `deploy/` | Docker Compose + Caddy for the production VPS |

## Dev setup

```bash
# uv: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv sync                      # creates .venv with all deps (Python 3.12)
cp .env.example .env         # fill in your own keys; never commit .env
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format .
uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port <your port>   # e.g. GET /api/health
```

On the shared team server, dev servers must use ports 3000-3099 or 8000-8099 (`je ports`).
Add dependencies with `uv add <pkg>` and commit `uv.lock`.

## Deploy

On the VPS, with `.env` at the repo root (set `PUBLIC_DOMAIN` for automatic HTTPS):

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml --env-file .env up -d --build
curl https://$PUBLIC_DOMAIN/api/health
```

All backend services share one image (`Dockerfile`); add a service in compose with its own
`command` (e.g. `python -m ingest`).

## Shared interfaces

Change these only with a note here, so the other components can follow.

**Database:** `db/schema.sql` (accounts, posts, reposts, follows, clusters, cluster_members,
cluster_posts, evidence, eval_runs). Cluster `status` is `coordinated | likely_organic | insufficient`;
evidence `kind` is `signal | media | source | analyst`.

**API** (JSON):
- `GET /api/health` → `{ok, ingest_lag_s, last_event_at}` *(implemented)*
- `GET /api/clusters?status=&min_score=&limit=` → cluster summaries
- `GET /api/clusters/{id}` → cluster + members + post sample + evidence + analyst verdict
- `GET /api/metrics` → latest `eval_runs` per dataset
- `POST /api/analyze` `{text?, url?, handle?}` → ad-hoc check

**Analyst verdict** (stored in `evidence.detail` with `kind='analyst'`):
```json
{"status": "coordinated|likely_organic|insufficient", "confidence": 0.0,
 "evidence": [{"evidence_id": 1, "why": "..."}],
 "counter_evidence": ["..."], "would_change_verdict": ["..."], "model": "gemini-..."}
```

**Env vars:** see `.env.example`.

## Rules

- Every number shown in the UI comes from `eval/` or `signals/` code, never hard-coded.
- Log every model call (model id, latency, tokens if returned).
- Read-only on Bluesky: never post or create accounts.

Base directory for this skill: /home/dev/.claude/skills/sol-loop

# sol-loop

This is a workflow for making your code changes more correct before (or
sometimes after) filing a pull request. tl;dr - use OpenAI's GPT Sol to review
your code in a loop.

Make the most minimal possible changes to appease the Sol reviewers. Be careful
of scope creep and don't be scared to push back.

## Budget

- Default: 3 rounds total. Round 1 is full. Later rounds check only
  changed code and open findings.
- Extend to 5 only for security, permissions, auth, data loss, or
  state/concurrency, while a blocker or should stays open with evidence. Or when
  the user asks.
- Stop early if a round returns only nits. Declined nits and comment,
  doc, or format-only fixes need no new round.
- One reviewer only. Sol must not start subagents or reviewers.
- Keep a ledger: id, severity, outcome, usage if returned. Never guess it.

## 1. Scope

Run `git status --short`. Do not stash, discard, or include unrelated
changes. Limit review to the change paths if they separate cleanly.
Otherwise stop and ask.

Find the base after `git fetch origin`:

- PR: `gh pr view <n> --json baseRefName,headRefOid`. Check out the branch
  only if clean. Confirm `HEAD` is the PR head, or ahead only by this
  change. Base: `git merge-base HEAD origin/<baseRefName>`.
- Local: `git merge-base HEAD origin/<default-branch>`. No remote: a base
  the user names, or `HEAD` for uncommitted changes only.

The change is base to working tree in those paths, with untracked files.
Use one diff command all rounds. State intent and out-of-scope in 1-2
sentences. Run covering checks. Do not send code this change breaks. Note
missing or pre-failing checks in the brief.

## 2. Start Sol

In T3, call `orchestrator_capabilities`. Pick the latest Sol unless the user
named a version. Do not hardcode an ID. Record provider, model, and effort
only if exposed. Use `delegate_task` every round (`role: "review"`,
`mode: "async"`). Save `taskId`. New `clientRequestId` per round.
`childThreadId` is storage, not the next target. Do not use
`t3_thread_send`, `create_threads`, or `t3_thread_launch` for review.

If T3 tools are not listed, try one direct capability call. Outside T3, use
a native Sol subagent and keep its ID. In Claude Code, use a custom subagent
only if it is set up to run Sol. If no route runs Sol, report the blocker. Do
not substitute a model.

Do not edit scoped files while review runs. Wait for the notice. Do not
poll or start a second reviewer. Timeout, error, or no reply is not
approval. On failure, cancel, verify stop, restart with the ledger.

Round 1 brief (T3 children get no history):

```
Review only. Do not edit, commit, push, comment on PRs, or start subagents.
Repo: <abs path> Base: <sha> Intent: <intent> Out of scope: <scope> Checks: <results>
See: git diff <base> [-- <paths>]; git status --short (read untracked).
Read surrounding code. Find bugs, broken callers, mismatch with intent.
Skip style unless it hides a bug. Hold to the smallest change. Flag code,
tests, or guards the intent does not need. Other paths, rare cases, small
perf, extra compat: nits.
blocker = intended case wrong. should = real bug callers will hit, in intent. nit = rest.
Reply:
VERDICT: APPROVE or CHANGES
S1 [blocker|should|nit] <file>:<line> <claim>. Fix: <suggestion> (stable ids)
```

## 3. Answer findings

Check each finding and severity yourself. Another path, rare case, or
small cost is a nit, whatever label it came with.

- Agree: smallest fix. Prefer delete or narrow over new lock, cache,
  helper, or option. Fix the case that happened. Add one focused test
  that fails without the fix, if intent needs it.
- Disagree: say why, with evidence (file:line, test, output).
- Out of scope or nit: decline in one line. List as follow-up.

Update the ledger. Re-run checks and `git diff --shortstat <base>`. If
review grew the diff, cut first. Do not agree just to end the loop.

## 4. Next round

Start one only if budget remains and a blocker or should is open, behavior code
changed, or approval does not cover the current behavior diff. Use a fresh
`delegate_task` in T3, or follow up the saved native ID. Send the round 1 brief,
the ledger (`fixed:` / `disagree:` / `declined:` + evidence), the same base
diff, and the change since last round. Tell Sol: open ids and changed code only.
Mark each old id `resolved` or `still open: <reason>`.

## 5. Stop and ship

Agreed: APPROVE on the current behavior diff, no blocker or should open,
no concern of your own. Stuck: an item stays disputed after two replies,
or budget ends. Show both sides in 2-3 lines each. The user decides.
Budget end is not approval.

Do not push during the loop. Push after agreement only if the user asked
to push, ship, or update the PR. If you push to a PR, add above the model
blurb:

`Reviewed with sol-loop: <N> rounds with <model>. Sol verdict: approved`.

Add `on <effort>` only if verified.

Report: rounds, model, what Sol changed, diff size before/after, fixed and
declined findings with reasons, usage if exposed (else say not), pushed or not.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Noise Radar

Detects coordinated amplification (bot or campaign behaviour) on Bluesky from behaviour signals,
explains each flagged cluster with evidence, and reports its own measured error rates.

## Layout

| Dir | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ingest/` | Bluesky Jetstream consumer → Postgres (`accounts`, `posts`, `reposts`, `follows`) |
| `signals/` | Coordination detector: windows, signals, clusters, score + confidence, abstention |
| `media/` | Nemotron Super VL: reads images/video frames, near-duplicate media |
| `sources/` | Oxylabs `/scrape` + `/search` on cluster links (source URLs kept with every fact) |
| `analyst/` | Gemini: per-cluster verdict with evidence and counter-evidence, or abstains |
| `eval/` | Precision / recall / F1 / FPR on held-out labelled data → `eval_runs` |
| `api/` | FastAPI backend |
| `web/` | Dashboard (`web/public/index.html` is a placeholder until the real app lands) |
| `common/` | Shared settings (`common.config`) and DB connections (`common.db`) |
| `db/schema.sql` | Database schema, applied by the Postgres container on first start |
| `deploy/` | Docker Compose + Caddy for the production VPS |

## Dev setup

```bash
# uv: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv sync                      # creates .venv with all deps (Python 3.12)
cp .env.example .env         # fill in your own keys; never commit .env
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format .
uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port <your port>   # e.g. GET /api/health
```

On the shared team server, dev servers must use ports 3000-3099 or 8000-8099 (`je ports`).
Add dependencies with `uv add <pkg>` and commit `uv.lock`.

## Deploy

On the VPS, with `.env` at the repo root (set `PUBLIC_DOMAIN` for automatic HTTPS):

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml --env-file .env up -d --build
curl https://$PUBLIC_DOMAIN/api/health
```

All backend services share one image (`Dockerfile`); add a service in compose with its own
`command` (e.g. `python -m ingest`).

## Entire (agent sessions, Graph, Brain)

The repo is set up for [Entire](https://docs.entire.com): Claude Code and Codex sessions are linked to
commits as checkpoints (stored under `refs/entire/checkpoints/` and pushed with your normal `git push`),
and `.entire/agent-guide.md` tells agents to use `entire graph` for code lookups.
The hooks do nothing until `entire` is on your PATH, so nothing breaks without it. To take part:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash   # installs entire into ~/.local/bin
entire login                                      # GitHub sign-in (use --device on a server)
entire plugin install graph && entire plugin install brain --yes
```

Then start a new agent session in your worktree. Checkpoints contain agent transcripts: never paste
keys or `.env` contents into a prompt. Committed Entire files: `.entire/settings.json`,
`.entire/.gitignore`, `.entire/agent-guide.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`,
`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` (Entire manages the marked blocks; add your own text outside them).

## Shared interfaces

Change these only with a note here, so the other components can follow.

**Database:** `db/schema.sql` (accounts, posts, reposts, follows, clusters, cluster_members,
cluster_posts, evidence, eval_runs). Cluster `status` is `coordinated | likely_organic | insufficient`;
evidence `kind` is `signal | media | source | analyst`.

**API** (JSON):
- `GET /api/health` → `{ok, ingest_lag_s, last_event_at}` *(implemented)*
- `GET /api/clusters?status=&min_score=&limit=` → cluster summaries
- `GET /api/clusters/{id}` → cluster + members + post sample + evidence + analyst verdict
- `GET /api/metrics` → latest `eval_runs` per dataset
- `POST /api/analyze` `{text?, url?, handle?}` → ad-hoc check

**Analyst verdict** (stored in `evidence.detail` with `kind='analyst'`):
```json
{"status": "coordinated|likely_organic|insufficient", "confidence": 0.0,
 "evidence": [{"evidence_id": 1, "why": "..."}],
 "counter_evidence": ["..."], "would_change_verdict": ["..."], "model": "gemini-..."}
```

**Env vars:** see `.env.example`.

## Rules

- Every number shown in the UI comes from `eval/` or `signals/` code, never hard-coded.
- Log every model call (model id, latency, tokens if returned).
- Read-only on Bluesky: never post or create accounts.

content.content:
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

Both backends act as ENTIRE_TOKEN when set, else the selected login
(--context, else $ENTIRE_CONTEXT, else the active context), so a staging
login reaches staging's control plane and cells. The cell host comes from
environment's cluster listing; an explicit ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL names the
data host directly instead.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (its processing placement) — cells key on this

With --to cell, a request whose path names {repo_id} goes to the cell that
hosts the repo instead of your home cell. /me/* paths and {repo_id} in the
query string stay on the home cell; --jurisdiction, and an ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL
naming a direct cell or local host, always win.

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

Both backends act as ENTIRE_TOKEN when set, else the selected login
(--context, else $ENTIRE_CONTEXT, else the active context), so a staging
login reaches staging's control plane and cells. The cell host comes from
environment's cluster listing; an explicit ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL names the
data host directly instead.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (its processing placement) — cells key on this

With --to cell, a request whose path names {repo_id} goes to the cell that
hosts the repo instead of your home cell. /me/* paths and {repo_id} in the
query string stay on the home cell; --jurisdiction, and an ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL
naming a direct cell or local host, always win.

Before filing, check whether a PR for this branch already exists. Review the

conventions. Look at recently merged PRs and Git history for examples. Prefer a

If model identity is unavailable, name the harness without guessing a model.

Before submission, check the title, description, quotes, and attachments for
secrets and private details.

Open a real PR rather than a draft so review bots run. If `gh pr create` fails
because the GraphQL rate limit is used up, open it through REST with

Base directory for this skill: /home/dev/.claude/skills/babysit-pr

# Babysit PR

Many repos have AI review bots. They're helpful, even if they are not always
right.

## Waiting

Never write your own watcher, polling loop, or `sleep` loop. Use one watcher
per PR: `watch_pull_request` in T3 Code, `pr-wait` everywhere else. Never run
both on the same PR. Every watcher on a GitHub account shares one rate limit.

### In T3 Code: `watch_pull_request`

Handle the existing checks and comments first. Then call
`watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you with a message when
a check fails, the required checks pass, someone comments or reviews, or the
branch conflicts.

- **Only the thread that owns the PR watches it.** If you are a delegated
  child task (a reviewer, a Sol round, any `delegate_task` child), never call
  `watch_pull_request`. The parent owns the PR. Do not watch PRs you are not
  working on.
- **A wake is news, not a merge decision.** Check the merge gate yourself.
- **Unwatch when you hand off.** A watched thread stays in Working and out of
  the user's inbox. When you stop (ready, blocked, or asking the user a question),
  call `unwatch_pull_request` first. A merge or close ends the watch on its
  own.
- **"Stopped watching, could not read it"** usually means GitHub's rate limit
  is used up. Run `gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql` before you
  watch again. If `remaining` is near 0, wait for `reset` with one background
  command, then watch again. Never watch again in a tight loop.

### Everywhere else: `pr-wait`

Wait with `scripts/pr-wait` from this skill's directory (use its absolute
path).

```bash
pr-wait <pr> [--repo owner/name] [--until ready|green|any-change]
```

It prints one line per real event. It exits 0 when the `--until` condition is
met or the PR merges, 1 when it needs you (a required check failed, conflicts,
unresolved threads, PR closed), and 2 on bad input.

- `ready` (default): required checks green, Greptile or Macroscope reviewed the
  head, and no unresolved threads. Use this to babysit.
- `green`: required checks only. Use it when the repo has no Greptile or
  Macroscope.
- `any-change`: exit on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it with the Monitor tool (`timeout_ms: 3600000`), so each
line wakes you. Without a monitor, run it as one long command. It ends on its
own.

Start it again after you push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume.
It remembers what it already reported, so nothing that arrived in between is
lost. If it says another pid already watches the PR, do not start a second one.
Kill the old one only if its events do not reach you.

With either watcher: when an event needs no action, end your turn without a
message. Never post or say "still waiting".

## GitHub rate limits

`gh pr create`, `gh pr view`, and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL. When GraphQL is
used up, the REST limit is separate and usually still has room. Use
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` to read a PR, and
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs` for checks.

## Reviews

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push. Verify every bot
finding against the source before changing code. Fix real findings and CI
failures, distinguish repository failures from infrastructure flakes, and reply
with a written reason when dismissing false positives.

If the repo has `.macroscope/check-run-agents/*.md`, read those rules before you
reply to a Macroscope finding. Its findings cite them.

CodeRabbit is advisory. Treat its findings like any other finding, but never
wait for it and never hold a merge for it.

If a review bot leaves feedback you believe is not worth addressing, reply with
a written reason and resolve the comment. Use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill
for every comment posted on the user's behalf.

Screenshots and videos help as well, when you have a way to upload them.

Keep the PR at the size the user's goal needs. Review loops tend to grow a
PR one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the intended case.
Decline the rest with a written reason, and list them as follow-ups:
unneeded tests, guards for edge cases that do not matter, extra integration
or compatibility, and small performance costs. Prefer the fix that deletes or
narrows code.

## Base branch and merging

Keep an eye on changes to `main` and rebase when needed. `pr-wait` reports when
new base commits touch this PR's files, and when the PR becomes BEHIND or DIRTY.
`watch_pull_request` reports conflicts only, so check for BEHIND yourself
before you call the PR ready.
If an overlapping PR makes this one obsolete, stop monitoring, report it to the
user, and ask before closing the PR unless closure was explicitly authorized.

If nothing has changed, stay quiet rather than posting filler comments. Stop
when `pr-wait` exits 0, or in T3 Code when the merge gate passes on the latest
head. Merge only when the user explicitly requested it;
otherwise report that the PR is ready. Right before a merge, run `git fetch` and
check the PR again. Never merge when it is BEHIND or DIRTY, or when base commits
that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files. Rebase, push, and
wait for green again.

Entire is set up and merged into `main`. You still need to redeem the MLH code and install the GitHub App yourself, because you told the nav thread agents must not do those.

**PR:** https://github.com/JustinasLa/gemini-4-braincells/pull/2, squash-merged as `5682723`. I also fast-forwarded the main checkout on the server so it has the change.

**What's live in the repo:**
- **Session checkpoints:** Claude Code and Codex sessions are saved with the commits they produce, and they push with a normal `git push`. I turned Entire's telemetry off.
- **Graph and Brain:** a new `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` points agents to `.entire/agent-guide.md`, which tells them to use `entire graph` to find code and `entire brain` to look up past decisions.
- **Safe for the others:** every hook does nothing if `entire` isn't installed, so commits and pushes keep working for the other seats. The README has the three install commands for teammates.
- **On the server:** the CLI is installed in `~/.local/bin` with the graph and brain plugins, and it's signed in as `github:JustinasLa`. The token is stored in `~/.config/entire/tokens.json` (owner-only), because the server has no keyring. That's why you had to approve a second time.

**Proof:**
- `pytest` and `ruff` pass.
- `entire doctor` reports the hooks are OK, and `entire status` shows Codex active after the merge.
- I made a commit through the installed git hooks and it went through normally.
- `entire graph query` found the `/api/health` handler.
- GPT-6.1 Sol reviewed the change twice and approved it after I fixed its two findings.

**Decisions I made:**
- Sol's first finding was real: Entire's push lock file in the shared `.git` was owner-only, so the other seats couldn't open it. I opened it to the `junction` group and pre-created a group-writable `.git/entire-sessions` folder.
- Codex users have to approve the hooks once with `/hooks` before capture works. I put that in the README.
- Brain is set up without the background watcher, and without importing past sessions, which costs model tokens.
- I added a line to `plan/DECISIONS.log`.

**Your steps:**
1. **Redeem `4PE349H9Q4`.** I couldn't find a redeem page in Entire's docs. **Account → Billing** at https://entire.com/account/billing is the likely place. Your billing shows "not started", and the docs say new free trials are paused, so the code is probably what unlocks credits.
2. **Install the Entire GitHub App** for `gemini-4-braincells` only. This is needed for mirrors and Trails.
3. **Teammates** each run the README install commands in their own seat.

Checkpoints contain full agent transcripts. The repo is private, but a session that reads `plan/` will carry that text into the checkpoints pushed to GitHub.

=== guides/repositories/mirrors
# Mirrors
> Connect an existing GitHub repository to Entire with an Entire-backed Git remote.
[Entire 101 | Ep. 3: What Is Mirroring a Repo Anyway?](https://www.youtube.com/embed/BkXpXdM5M7E)
## What Is a Mirror?
A mirror is a synchronized copy of your repository. The origin remains on GitHub, but the copy lives on Entire in one or more regional clusters of your choice. This allows you to offload heavy read traffic to Entire, enabling your agents to pull and clone faster.
Entire represents the GitHub repository as a single repository object. Each region you mirror into is a mirror placement, which connects that object to one Entire cluster. If you mirror the same repository in two regions, you have one repository object and two mirror placements, each with its own `entire://` URL.
## Why Use a Mirror
Mirroring is helpful when you or your agents need faster Git reads close to where they run.
* you want your agents to keep cloning and pulling during a GitHub outage
## Before You Create a Mirror
The [Entire GitHub App must be able to access the repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md) before you can create a mirror. After that, anyone with access to the GitHub repository can create a mirror from entire.com or with the Entire CLI.
You should choose regions based on where your agents run and where your organization allows code to live. Each region you select becomes a separate mirror placement.
If a repository has mirrors in more than one region, `entire repo clone` and `entire repo remote add` ask you to choose one. Without a terminal a GitHub mirror falls back to `aws-us-east-2.entire.io` and errors if it is not placed there, so pass `--cluster` in scripts, or `--nearest` to have `entire repo clone` pick the fastest.
## Create a Mirror
There are multiple ways to create a mirror, here’s how:
* To create a mirror from entire.com, read [Mirrors in entire.com](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-entire-com.md).
* To create one from the terminal, head to [Mirrors in CLI](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli.md).
* For a full walkthrough, see [Mirror a GitHub Repository](https://docs.entire.com/learn/mirror-a-github-repository.md).
Creating a mirror gives you:
* a synced Entire copy of your GitHub repository
* an Entire access list that syncs from GitHub every hour
You can clone directly from the mirror or add it as another remote in an existing checkout.
Creating a mirror does not:
* move, delete, or replace the GitHub repository
* require every developer to change remotes
=== guides/repositories/entire-native-branches
# Entire-Native Branches
> Push branches that stay on Entire when GitHub is down.
## What Is an Entire-Native Branch?
When you mirror a repository with Entire, it stays in sync with GitHub as its primary origin. You clone and fetch from a regional Entire mirror, but every push still routes to GitHub. By design, pushes are only as fast as GitHub allows, and when there is an outage, you cannot push at all.
Entire-native branches let you keep pushing during an outage and absorb the heavy write traffic of agent workflows. Use one when you have several agents working in parallel, or when you need pushes to be fast. An Entire-native branch skips the sync with GitHub and stays on Entire, in the region that hosts your repository.
## Push to an Entire-Native Branch
To enable an Entire-native branch, you just need to name your branch with the `entire/unmirrored/` prefix and push as usual:
git switch -c entire/unmirrored/agent-work
git push origin entire/unmirrored/agent-work
> These examples assume `origin` points at your Entire mirror, which is what `entire repo remote add origin --override` does. If you added Entire alongside GitHub with `entire repo remote add entire`, push to `entire` instead of `origin`.
When asked to push to Entire (not GitHub), push to a branch named
`entire/unmirrored/<task-name>`. When asked to publish to GitHub,
> Push this to Entire, not GitHub.
When you want it on GitHub:
> Publish this to GitHub.
The agent handles the branch names. Native branches stay on Entire until you publish them. And you can continue coding and pushing even when GitHub is down.
Entire-native branches don't sync to GitHub automatically. When you are ready to bring the work into your GitHub repo, push it again under a normal branch name without any prefix:
You still need write access to push, the same as with any mirrored branch. Entire checks this against the collaborator access it copies from GitHub. Entire picks up access changes when GitHub reports them, and a background sync re-reads collaborators at least once a day to catch any it missed. Because these pushes never reach GitHub, a user whose GitHub access was removed can still push to these branches until Entire picks up that change. See [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md) for how that sync works.
## Limitations
* Entire does not currently back up Entire-native branches, so if you need to keep the work for a longer time, you need to save a copy somewhere else too.
